entries.clue: Discards hospital attire (6)

blocks.note: the verb sense: to scrub a plan is to cancel it and throw it away
the plural noun: the loose cotton top and trousers worn in an operating theatre

annotation.surface: Somebody is throwing out the clothes they wore on the ward.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are common, but they sit in different grammatical boxes — one a verb, one a plural noun — so the clue reads as a single sentence. Surgeons change into the second before an operation.
annotation.definitionFit: To scrub an arrangement is to cancel it, and the loose cotton tunic and trousers a surgeon works in carry the same name.

entries.clue: Claret’s alternative red (7)

indicatorNotes.alternative: An alternative version of something is the same material arranged another way, which is licence to reorder these letters.

blocks.note: seven letters to rearrange, apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A wine drinker is being offered a different red instead of claret.
annotation.walkthrough: Claret is red bordeaux, so the word sits in the surface as a drink and in the parse as raw material. The apostrophe is punctuation only and contributes nothing to the count.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer is one particular bright shade of red, offered here under the general colour word as a definition by example.

entries.clue: Agent penning account, upsetting summary (5)

indicatorNotes.penning: To pen an animal is to shut it inside a pen, so the first word closes round what comes next.
indicatorNotes.upsetting: Upsetting a thing stands it on its head, and in a down entry that writes those two letters bottom to top.

blocks.note: a rep is an agent, the one who calls to sell you something, and it opens up to take the insert
account shortens to AC, here stood on its head

annotation.surface: An agent quietly writing up an account produces a distressing summary.
annotation.walkthrough: The turning applies only to the two letters of the account, not to the agent wrapped round them, and getting that scope wrong is the usual wrong turn here. Both halves are short, which is what makes a five-letter entry this fiddly.
annotation.definitionFit: A recap goes back over ground already covered in a few words, which is what a summary does at the end of a meeting.

entries.clue: Big actors in TV show? (9)

blocks.note: broad means big across, as in broad shoulders
the cast is the whole company of actors in a production

annotation.surface: A television programme has landed itself some big-name actors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Big' looks as though it is describing the actors, and prising it away from them is the entire difficulty. The question mark concedes that a television programme is only one of the things sent out this way.
annotation.definitionFit: Anything transmitted over the air is a broadcast, and a television programme is exactly that, offered here as one instance of the wider word.

entries.clue: Exerted force on journalists and editor (7)

blocks.note: the press is the body of journalists taken collectively, as in press conference
ed is the standard short form of editor

annotation.surface: Someone has been leaning on a newspaper's reporters and their editor.
annotation.walkthrough: On the surface the journalists are on the receiving end of the pressure; in the wordplay they supply five letters and nothing is done to them at all. Newspapers are called the press because of the machine that printed them.
annotation.definitionFit: To press someone is to push or lean on them, and the past tense of that verb is what exerting force amounts to.

entries.clue: Entertainer with requests, entertainer completely gutted (7)

indicatorNotes.completely gutted: Gutting a thing takes out its insides, and doing it completely leaves nothing behind but the first and last letters.

blocks.note: pleas are urgent requests
the clue's second performer keeps only its outer pair, ten letters thrown away from between them

annotation.surface: Two performers, one fielding requests and the other left utterly hollow.
annotation.walkthrough: The same word does both jobs: it defines the answer at the start of the clue and is raw material at the end. A solver who has settled the first word rarely goes back to look at it again.
annotation.definitionFit: A pleaser is a person or turn that gives a crowd pleasure, which is what an entertainer is hired to do.

entries.clue: Expunge article in Irish language (5)

indicatorNotes.in: Putting one thing in another is exactly where the article goes — surrounded by the language, not standing beside it.

blocks.note: Erse is the old name for Irish Gaelic
a is the indefinite article

annotation.surface: An editor is deleting a piece written in the Irish tongue.
annotation.walkthrough: Erse turns up in crosswords far more often than in conversation, and learning it saves a great deal of time. 'Article' is the grammarian's kind here, not the newspaper's.
annotation.definitionFit: To erase is to rub something out so no trace is left, and expunging is the same removal named in more formal language.

entries.clue: Eastern females needing external protection in Yorkshire city (9)

indicatorNotes.external: What is external sits on the outside, so the protecting word wraps round the letters instead of joining them end to end.

blocks.note: a shield is protection, the piece of armour rather than a bodyguard
e is the compass abbreviation for eastern
f stands for female, and the plural doubles the letter

annotation.surface: Women from the East are in need of protection from outside.
annotation.walkthrough: Doubling a letter to make it plural — f for female, ff for females — is a standard move worth banking. The shield opens after only two of its own letters, which is an awkward split to spot.
annotation.definitionFit: Sheffield sits in South Yorkshire and is that county's largest city, long the centre of English steel and cutlery.

entries.clue: Readily working, one coming out at great cost (6)

indicatorNotes.working: Something working is in motion, and letters in motion do not stay in the order they were handed over in.
indicatorNotes.coming out: What comes out leaves the word it was sitting in, so that letter is gone before anything else happens.

blocks.note: the seven-letter word with its fourth letter taken away, leaving six to rearrange
one is the Roman numeral I, the letter that departs

annotation.surface: A willing worker comes out about something and pays a heavy price for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coming out' has to be read as a removal, and the surface's other sense buries that completely. One is the Roman numeral here, a single letter, which is the only reading that leaves six behind for the count.
annotation.definitionFit: To pay dearly for something is to pay a lot for it, the adverb keeping the sense of expense rather than of affection.

entries.clue: Vehicle with chaps in opera (6)

blocks.note: a car is the everyday vehicle
chaps is the British word for men

annotation.surface: A car full of blokes is turning up at the opera.
annotation.walkthrough: Bizet's opera is named after its gypsy heroine, and the clue's two ordinary words sit inside her name untouched. 'Chaps' is simply British for blokes.
annotation.definitionFit: Carmen is Bizet's opera about a cigarette girl in Seville, so naming a work by its title answers the general word for the form.

entries.clue: Place for vehicles to stop in Alaskan port (9)

blocks.note: the general sense: sheltered water where a ship may lie at anchor
the proper noun: the city on Cook Inlet, Alaska's largest

annotation.surface: Somewhere for cars to pull up in a town on the Alaskan coast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vehicles' does the misdirecting: you picture a car park, and the ships that actually stop there never come to mind. The two definitions run straight into each other with only a preposition between them.
annotation.definitionFit: An anchorage is sheltered water where a ship can drop anchor and wait, and the Alaskan city of that name is the state's main seaport.

entries.clue: Stadium zone accommodating small number (5)

indicatorNotes.accommodating: To accommodate a guest is to take them in and find them room, so the letter goes inside the word before it.

blocks.note: a zone is an area, and it parts near the end to take a letter
n is the mathematician's stand-in for some unspecified quantity, written as a small letter

annotation.surface: A section of the ground is holding only a handful of spectators.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface welds 'zone' onto the stadium, so the two read as one phrase rather than as a definition sitting next to its wordplay. N for an unstated number comes straight from algebra.
annotation.definitionFit: An arena is the enclosed space a crowd watches sport or spectacle in, which is what a stadium is built to provide.

entries.clue: Ran, being guided outside work (5)

indicatorNotes.outside: What is outside surrounds what is inside, so the guided word closes round the two letters it is given.

blocks.note: someone being guided is led
op is short for opus, a composer's numbered work

annotation.surface: Somebody jogged with a guide alongside, outside of working hours.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outside work' reads as one phrase about the office, which is exactly the join the setter wants you to miss. A three-letter word splitting after its first letter is the hardest kind of container to see.
annotation.definitionFit: To lope is to run with a long, easy, bounding stride, so the past tense of the plain verb covers it.

entries.clue: Domineering maiden has ‘er faults unfortunately (9)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: When something goes unfortunately it does not come out as arranged, and letters that refuse to stay as arranged must be reordered.

blocks.note: m is the cricket scorer's mark for a maiden, an over from which no runs are scored
a dropped-aitch 'her faults', eight letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A young woman is being told her shortcomings, sad to say.
annotation.walkthrough: That opening apostrophe is doing real work, marking a dropped aitch so 'her' arrives two letters short. Missing it costs you an H the grid has no room for.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone masterful takes charge and expects to be obeyed, which is the overbearing quality the definition names.

entries.clue: Piece of ground in second half of season needing wet weather (7)

indicatorNotes.second half of: Taking the second half of a word keeps its back portion and throws the front away.

blocks.note: winter is the season whose back half is TER; spring, summer and autumn lead nowhere
wet weather is rain

annotation.surface: A pitch late in the season is crying out for rain.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter leaves 'season' unspecified, so you try all four and only winter's back half goes anywhere. The surface sells the whole thing as one phrase about a playing surface late in the campaign.
annotation.definitionFit: Terrain is a stretch of land considered for its lie and surface, which is what calling something a piece of ground amounts to.

entries.clue: Chemical processes bringing responses (9)

blocks.note: the laboratory sense: what happens when substances are put together
the human sense: what people say or feel when something is put to them

annotation.surface: Processes in a laboratory are producing results worth remarking on.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as cause and effect, which disguises the fact that its two halves are the same word twice over. Chemistry and conversation are the two worlds that word lives in.
annotation.definitionFit: A reaction is both what happens when substances combine and what a person gives back when prodded — one word covering flask and conversation alike.

entries.clue: Greek character pinned by exceptionally rare sword (6)

indicatorNotes.pinned by: To be pinned by something is to be held fast under it, so the Greek letter ends up surrounded rather than tacked on.
indicatorNotes.exceptionally: What is done exceptionally departs from the usual order, and these letters depart from theirs.

blocks.note: four letters to rearrange, parting to let the other two in
pi is the sixteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

annotation.surface: A Greek is held down by the point of an unusually rare sword.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' is the letter kind, not the person the surface offers you, and pi is the two-letter one setters reach for. The four letters it lands among do not keep their given order either.
annotation.definitionFit: A rapier is the slender thrusting blade of the duelling era, so the general word for such a weapon covers it.

entries.clue: Servant admitting fiery crime in minister’s home (9)

indicatorNotes.admitting: To admit someone is to let them in at the door, so the crime goes inside the servant rather than after him.

blocks.note: a page is a young servant in a great household
arson is the crime of deliberately setting fire to property

annotation.surface: A servant is confessing to setting a fire at the vicarage.
annotation.walkthrough: The servant splits after a single letter, and a one-letter opening is the hardest kind to notice. A parson is a Church of England clergyman, and the house his parish gives him takes his name.
annotation.definitionFit: A parsonage is the dwelling a parish provides for its parson, who is the minister of that church.

entries.clue: Bishop and former PM endlessly struggle (6)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Something endless has no end, so the politician's name arrives without its final letter.

blocks.note: b is the chess notation for a bishop
Clement Attlee, Labour prime minister from 1945, docked of his last letter

annotation.surface: A bishop and an ex-prime minister are locked in an unending fight.
annotation.walkthrough: Attlee led the Labour government that founded the National Health Service, and his name is a crossword regular for its run of convenient letters. B for bishop comes from the chessboard, not the church.
annotation.definitionFit: To battle is to fight hard and at length against something, which is exactly what struggling against it means.

entries.clue: Familiar territory for copper perhaps (7)

blocks.note: the idiomatic sense: the surroundings a person is at home in and works best in
the chemical sense; 'perhaps' marks copper as one substance of the kind, not the whole class

annotation.surface: A policeman is back on the streets he knows best.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper is the policeman on the surface and the metal in the parse, and that single switch is the clue. Being in your element is the idiom the first half leans on.
annotation.definitionFit: Being in your element means being where you are comfortable, and copper is one of the chemical elements, flagged as an example by 'perhaps'.

entries.clue: Shorten a card game (7)

blocks.note: the clue's own article, taken across as a letter
bridge is the partnership card game descended from whist

annotation.surface: A game of cards is being cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one instruction, so nothing prompts you to break the article off from what follows. Bridge is a card game here and not a structure, which is the sense the rest of the sentence supplies.
annotation.definitionFit: To abridge a book is to cut it down to a shorter version, so shortening names precisely that act.

entries.clue: King showing skill. monarch finally coming to old city (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: What comes finally is the last of its line, so only the closing letter of the word before it is taken.

blocks.note: art is skill, as in the art of conversation
the closing letter of monarch
Ur was the great city of ancient Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq

annotation.surface: A king's skill is on display as he reaches an ancient city at last.
annotation.walkthrough: Ur is the standard crossword old city, familiar from the Old Testament as Abraham's birthplace. The definition works by example: one famous holder of the title, not kingship in general.
annotation.definitionFit: Arthur is the legendary British king of Camelot, so the bare title offers the category and one celebrated bearer of it fills the grid.

entries.clue: Collapsed in seat, hugging love in the country (7)

indicatorNotes.Collapsed: A collapsed structure has lost the arrangement it was built in, which is the invitation to rebuild these letters another way.
indicatorNotes.hugging: A hug closes the arms right round someone, so the rebuilt letters go round the single one that follows.

blocks.note: six letters to rearrange, parting to take one more
love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

annotation.surface: Someone has slumped into a chair out in the countryside, clutching their sweetheart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the country' reads as scenery and is in fact the definition, so the join sits later in the sentence than it looks. Estonia is the northernmost of the three Baltic states, facing Finland across the gulf.
annotation.definitionFit: Estonia is a sovereign nation on the Baltic, offered here under the plain word for any such state as a definition by example.

entries.clue: Healthy Edward given appropriate kit? (6)

blocks.note: someone fit is in good health
Ted is the familiar form of Edward

annotation.surface: A healthy man called Edward has been issued with the right gear.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark covers a definition that is a whole phrase rather than a one-word synonym, so you are hunting a word meaning kitted out. Ted for Edward is the everyday nickname, not a crossword convention.
annotation.definitionFit: A ship or a soldier fitted out has been supplied with the proper equipment, which is what being handed the right gear comes to.

entries.clue: Bury group, about a hundred, becoming cross (9)

indicatorNotes.about: Something placed about a thing lies round the outside of it, so the group closes over the numeral.

blocks.note: to inter a body is to bury it
a set is a group, and it parts before its last letter
C is the Roman hundred

annotation.surface: A hundred or so people from Bury are getting angry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' is angry on the surface and crossing in the answer, which is where the humour sits. Bury is a Lancashire town as well as a verb, and the capital letter at the head of the clue keeps that reading alive.
annotation.definitionFit: Two roads that intersect run across each other at a point, so the plain verb to cross names the same action.

entries.clue: Get up about middle of morning and wash (5)

indicatorNotes.about: Placed about something means placed round it, so the first word closes over what it is given.
indicatorNotes.middle of: The middle of a word is its central letter, the one with the same number of letters either side.

blocks.note: to get up in the morning is to rise
the central letter of the seven in morning

annotation.surface: Someone gets out of bed around mid-morning and has a wash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get up' is the plain rising here, not an instruction to turn the entry round, which is the first thing to test in a down clue. Morning has seven letters, so its middle is a single one.
annotation.definitionFit: To rinse is to wash something through with clean water, so the general verb covers this particular kind of it.

entries.clue: Attack with stone being thrown (5)

indicatorNotes.being thrown: A thing thrown lands where it will rather than in the order it left, and these letters do the same.

blocks.note: five letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: Somebody is being pelted with a rock.
annotation.walkthrough: The stone really is thrown on the surface, so the instruction passes as part of the picture rather than as an order. An onset is the launching of an attack as much as the attack itself.
annotation.definitionFit: An onset is an assault begun, and the plain noun for that assault carries the same sense of a force coming at you.

entries.clue: Move and keep quiet if having little time (5)

blocks.note: sh is the noise made to hush somebody
the clue's own word, carried across unchanged
t is the standard short form of time, the little bit of the word

annotation.surface: Somebody is told to stay silent if they are pressed for time.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue's own 'if' goes straight into the answer unaltered, which solvers skip past while hunting for something cleverer. Sh is spelt as the two letters you actually make when hushing a room.
annotation.definitionFit: To shift a thing is to move it from where it stands, the same action the plain verb names.

entries.clue: Old English character conveyed by author naturally (5)

indicatorNotes.conveyed by: What is conveyed by something is carried along inside it, so the letters sit unbroken in the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts four letters into the first word and finishes one letter into the second

annotation.surface: A writer is passing something on perfectly naturally.
annotation.walkthrough: Thorn is the runic letter þ that Old English used for the 'th' sound, and it survives in the fake 'Ye' of mock-Tudor shop signs. 'Character' means letter here, not person.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer is the name of the runic letter þ that wrote the 'th' sound in Old English manuscripts, so it is literally one of that language's letters.

entries.clue: Action due to change in school activity (9)

indicatorNotes.to change: What is due to change will not stay as it is, and letters that will not stay put have to be set down in a new order.

blocks.note: nine letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: Something planned is due to be altered during a school activity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Due to change' reads as bureaucratic scheduling, which is exactly why the instruction goes unnoticed. The fodder sits at the very front of the clue, where solvers look for a definition first.
annotation.definitionFit: Education is what schools exist to deliver, so naming the thing a school is for describes it directly.

entries.clue: Sweet son stuck in Sahara? (7)

indicatorNotes.stuck in: Something stuck in a place cannot get out of it, so the letter lodges inside the word rather than beside it.

blocks.note: the Sahara is a desert, the largest hot one on earth, and the question mark flags the example
s is the standard short form of son

annotation.surface: A boy is stranded in the Sahara.
annotation.walkthrough: Desert and dessert differ by one s, and the clue is built entirely on that gap. Sweet is the British name for the pudding course at the end of a meal.
annotation.definitionFit: In British usage the sweet is the course that closes dinner, the same one a restaurant menu lists under this longer name.

entries.clue: Woman in the bar, sozzled (6)

indicatorNotes.sozzled: Sozzled means thoroughly drunk, and a drunk keeps nothing in a straight line, letters included.

blocks.note: six letters to rearrange

annotation.surface: A woman is propping up the bar, thoroughly drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sozzled' belongs to the picture as much as to the wordplay, which is what makes it easy to read straight past. Bertha is an old-fashioned first name, best known now from the Big Bertha gun.
annotation.definitionFit: The answer is a woman's given name, offered under the bare word for a female person as a definition by example.
